## What an analyst of the robustness study received {#what-an-analyst-received .smaller}

::: {.small}
- A **published paper**, in full and not blinded, so I could see the original estimates
- Its **central claim**, in one sentence, lifted from the abstract
- A pointer to the **data** – in our case, sixteen Eurobarometer waves you fetch yourself from GESIS
- No instructions on method – any analysis you can defend
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
And two things I was not told: **who the other analysts were**, and **what they were finding**.
:::

::: {.src}
The SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]; its preregistration, osf.io/4ev9t, pp. 4–5.
:::

::: notes
The SCORE robustness study gave a hundred published studies to at least five independent analysts each, and I was one of those analysts, so I can describe it from the inside, which shapes how you read the results. I received the whole published paper, not blinded, with the original estimates in view, which if anything pulls an analyst towards the original answer. With it came the central claim of the paper in a single sentence, taken from the abstract, and a pointer to the data, in our case sixteen Eurobarometer waves that I had to fetch from GESIS myself, under licence. No instruction on method arrived, beyond analysing the data in any way that I could defend. [advance] And two things stayed hidden throughout, who the other analysts were and what they were finding, an isolation that belonged to the design, since it gives the spread at the end its meaning.
:::

## The paper in brief {#the-paper-for-now-in-one-slide}

::: {.small}
- Author: I will say **OA**, the original author, from here on

::: {.claimcard}
"The results show, first, that *poor economic performances* **increase negative** and **decrease positive** *dimensions of EU framing*."
:::
:::

::: {.src}
@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic. The full methodological reading comes later in the workshop.
:::

::: notes
The paper appeared in 2016 in the European Sociological Review, and I refer to its author as the original author. The claim that we were handed is the sentence in the box, and later in the workshop we take the paper apart.
:::

## The two tasks of the robustness study {#two-tasks-months-apart .smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 1 – free reanalysis.** Reanalyse the claim however you see fit. Record one categorical conclusion: does the evidence support it?

::: {.fragment}
**Task 2 – constrained reanalysis.** Once Task 1 was in, four instructions arrived: one main result as a z-, t-, F- or $\chi^2$ test, no contextual variables on EU policies or the parties, the **positive non-materialist form of EU framing** as the outcome, and the **unemployment rate** as the measure of poor economic performance.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Task 1 measures whether we agree. Task 2 makes our *numbers* comparable – you cannot average five answers to five different questions.
:::

::: notes
The study ran in two stages, and the distinction matters for everything that follows. Task 1 left us free to reanalyse the claim in any way that we thought fit and asked for one categorical conclusion on whether the evidence supports it. [advance] Once that was submitted, Task 2 arrived with four instructions, which we read word for word in Part 3: one main result as a single test statistic, no contextual variables on EU policies or the parties, the positive non-materialist form of EU framing, which is the cosmopolitan scale of the paper, as the outcome, and the unemployment rate as the measure of poor economic performance. [advance] The two tasks measure different things. Task 1 asks whether independent analysts reach the same verdict, and Task 2 whether they produce the same number, a question that can only be asked once everyone answers the same question, which is what the instructions were for.
:::

## Results on a common scale {#how-a-hundred-studies-become-one-number .smaller}

::: {.small}
- Every analyst reports their test statistic and its degrees of freedom, in whatever form their model produces – **t**, **z**, **F**, $\chi^2$
- Each is converted to a **partial correlation** *r* and a standardised **Cohen's *d***, so a fixed-effects model fitted in Stata and a multilevel model fitted in R can be read on the same axis
- A **peer panel** judges whether each pipeline is an appropriate analysis of the claim
- Only then can you ask: how far apart are five defensible answers?
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Standardising makes the comparison possible, but it assumes that the five are estimating **the same quantity**, and that the degrees of freedom behind each conversion count the units that carry the evidence. Hold both thoughts.
:::

::: notes
Even with the question pinned down, the answers arrive in different forms, since each analyst reports the test statistic that the model produces, a t, a z, an F or a chi-squared, with its degrees of freedom. The statistics are converted to a common scale, a partial correlation and a standardised mean difference, so that a fixed-effects model fitted in Stata and a multilevel model fitted in R can be read on the same axis. A panel of peers also judged whether each analysis was appropriate for the claim, so the spread on the next slide is a spread among analyses that passed review. [advance] Putting five numbers on one axis takes two things for granted, that the five estimate the same quantity, which the part on estimands takes up, and that the degrees of freedom fed into each conversion count the units that carry the evidence, which the next chart puts to the test.
:::


## The five analysts – Task 2 results {#our-five-one-sign-very-different-sizes .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: forest5
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 4.1
# The five analysts of the robustness study on the same claim (data/reference_marks.csv, with
# the software and document format from data/analysts5.csv), each placed on
# the degrees of freedom of its own inference; an open circle marks the value
# in the record of the robustness study where it differs, which is PRL47 alone, converted on
# its respondent count. C6HJR highlighted. The label shows the software and
# the document format, because this chart also leads into the tools segment:
# the toolchain did not cause the spread, but every analyst shipped a
# runnable document, which is what made the spread diagnosable afterwards.
tools5 <- analysts5 |> dplyr::select(id = analyst_id, tool, document)
fa <- ref_marks |>
  dplyr::filter(id != "OA") |>
  dplyr::left_join(tools5, by = "id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    me      = id == "C6HJR",
    lab     = paste0(id, "   ", tool, "  ", document),
    differs = abs(r_recorded - r_placement) > 0.001
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(r_placement) |>
  dplyr::mutate(lab = factor(lab, levels = lab))
fa_rec <- dplyr::filter(fa, differs)

ggplot2::ggplot(fa, ggplot2::aes(r_placement, lab)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = grey_mid, linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(data = fa_rec, ggplot2::aes(x = r_recorded, xend = r_placement, yend = lab),
               colour = grey_mid, linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "dotted") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = fa_rec, ggplot2::aes(x = r_recorded), shape = 21, size = 5.5,
             colour = grey_mid, fill = "white", stroke = 1.1) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(data = fa_rec, ggplot2::aes(x = r_recorded, label = sprintf("recorded %s", fmt_num(r_recorded))),
            vjust = -1.3, hjust = 1.05, size = 4, colour = grey_mid) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(colour = me), size = 6) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = paste("r =", fmt_num(r_placement, 2))),
            hjust = 1.3, size = 4.5, colour = ncl_blue) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = ncl_blue, `TRUE` = orange)) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.62, 0.06), labels = \(x) fmt_num(x, 1)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "partial correlation r, on the degrees of freedom of each inference",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(15)
```

::: {.small}
- All five estimates negative, with partial *r* from **`r fmt_num(min(five_r), 2)` to `r fmt_num(max(five_r), 2)`**, and one of the five not significant even by the errors of its own model
- The robustness study recorded PRL47 at *r* = `r fmt_num(mark_of("PRL47", "r_recorded"))` (open circle), because its *z* was converted on `r format(analysts5$n[analysts5$analyst_id == "PRL47"], big.mark = ",")` respondents
:::

::: {.src}
Task 2 results as recorded in the public dataset of the robustness study (osf.io/q5h2c); PRL47 placed on the `r fmt_num(mark_of("PRL47", "df_placement"), 1)` Satterthwaite df of the workshop's refit of its design (data/reference_marks.csv).
:::

::: notes
These are the five of us on this one claim. All five found a negative association, and the sizes run from minus point zero six, not significant even by the errors of its own model, to minus point four five, more than seven times as large, with my own result, the orange dot, at minus point two four. The open circle on the row of PRL47 is the value recorded by the robustness study, minus point zero zero six, because its z was converted on the number of respondents, as if each respondent were an independent test of a national unemployment rate, while the filled dot puts the same statistic on the degrees of freedom of the workshop's refit of its design, at minus point one eight. As recorded, the five values spanned nearly two orders of magnitude, mostly because of that conversion. Before we turn to the rest of the spread, look at the labels down the left-hand side.
:::

## Software and document formats {#look-at-the-labels .smaller}

::: {.small}
- Two of us worked in **Stata**, three in **R**
- Within R, three different document formats: a plain `.R` script, an `.Rmd`, a `.qmd`
:::

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
The software did **not** cause the spread. There is no Stata answer and no R answer to this claim.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
But because each of us submitted a document that somebody else could **open and run**, it became possible, afterwards, to find out what *did* cause it.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
That is what the toolchain is for.
:::
::::

::: notes
Two of the five worked in Stata and three in R, and within R in three different document formats, a plain script, an R Markdown file and a Quarto file. [advance] The software did not cause the spread, since every one of these models can be fitted in either language, so there is no Stata answer and no R answer to this claim. [advance] The column matters for another reason. Because each of us submitted a document that somebody else could open and run, it became possible afterwards to find out what did cause the spread, and I have read the code of the other four line by line. Later today you work through the same choices that they faced. [advance]
:::
